lines.text: You will hear a presenter on a local radio station talking about a city arts week. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: Good morning, and welcome back to The Morning Mix on Riverton Community Radio. If you've walked through the city centre lately, you'll have seen the banners going up, because Riverton Arts Week starts this Saturday.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: The festival's actually longer this year, nine days instead of the usual seven, so there's plenty of time to fit things in. I've been looking through the programme, and I want to pick out a few highlights for you.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: Let's start with the lantern parade on the opening night. It follows the same route as always, from the old bridge up to Market Square. What's different this year is that you don't have to just stand and watch. The organisers are running lantern-making sessions all week, where you can make your own lantern, and then you can walk in the parade with it.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: Next, the photography exhibition, which is called City at Night. In previous years the exhibition has always been held in the museum, but the museum's being renovated, so this year it'll be in the old tram depot on Foundry Lane. Entry's five dollars, and it's open daily from ten until six.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: If music's more your thing, there's the jazz evening in the botanic gardens on the Wednesday. Last year it ran over two nights, but it's just the one this time. Tickets are 15 dollars, and please bring your own picnic, because there's no food on sale.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: The important thing to know is that there are only 300 seats, and you won't be able to buy tickets at the gate. You have to reserve them on the festival website before the night.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: For families, the Paper Moon puppet company is back at the Kingsway Theatre. Their show this year is a gentle one, designed especially for toddlers and pre-school children, so it's probably a bit young for anyone over six. Tickets are four dollars, and you can just turn up on the day. There's no café in the building, though, so you might want to bring a snack.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: And finally in this part of the programme, there's the storytelling night at the Central Library, which has been held there every year since the festival began. In the past, members of the public could get up and tell a story themselves, but sadly the organisers have dropped the open-mic section, so this year you'll just be listening. The good news is that there's no charge at all, and you don't need a ticket.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: Now, a few practical points. If you'd like a copy of the full programme, it's online, of course. But if you prefer paper, printed copies are available at any public library. They used to be handed out at the tourist information centre as well, but the centre's closed for refurbishment this month, so don't go there.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: Getting around should be easy. The buses are running their normal timetable, so the last one leaves the city centre at about half past eleven. But the city council has arranged for the trams to keep running until one in the morning on both Saturdays, so that's the best way home after the late events.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: There's also a new sculpture trail along the riverbank this year, with twelve pieces by local artists. It's about four kilometres long, and I walked it last weekend. A word of warning, though. Some of the path still hasn't been surfaced, and after all the rain we've had, it's very muddy in places.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: I saw people trying it in trainers and having a miserable time. You'll really need walking boots.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: Now, for any young artists listening, there's a drawing competition for children aged five to twelve. The theme is My Favourite Place in Riverton, and entries need to be handed in at the library by the first Friday.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: In past years the prize has been a tablet computer, but the organisers felt that didn't really suit an arts festival. So this year the winner will get a term of art lessons at the Riverside Studio, which I think is a lovely idea.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: And the week finishes, as always, with fireworks over the harbour. They were originally planned for the final Saturday night. But that's when the harbour's hosting the sailing regatta, and the boats won't be cleared away in time, so the fireworks have been moved to Sunday, starting at nine o'clock. The forecast looks good, so fingers crossed.

lines.speaker: presenter
lines.text: That's all from me on Arts Week for now. I'll be talking to some of the artists later in the week, so stay tuned. And after the break, we'll have the weather and the traffic.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of the recording. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
